report:
## Conclusion: The claim is not supported by human evidence

Capsaicin (the compound that makes chili peppers hot) shows promising **anti-cancer activity in laboratory studies** — killing breast cancer cells in petri dishes and shrinking tumors in mice — but there is **no clinical evidence that it treats breast cancer in humans**. The claim as stated ("capsaicin treats breast cancer in humans") is therefore **unproven and misleading**.

### Evidence supporting the underlying idea (preclinical only)

- Multiple *in vitro* studies show capsaicin induces apoptosis and cell-cycle arrest in breast cancer cell lines such as MCF-7 and MDA-MB-231, and can synergize with other compounds like genistein. These are laboratory findings, not human trials. (https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/oncology/articles/10.3389/fonc.2022.908487/full; https://www.dovepress.com/capsaicin-inhibits-proliferation-and-induces-apoptosis-in-breast-cance-peer-reviewed-fulltext-article-DDDT)
- A 2016 review in *Anticancer Research* describes capsaicin's proposed mechanisms — apoptosis, anti-angiogenesis, anti-metastasis — but notes these are based on experimental/epidemiological evidence, not established therapy. (https://ar.iiarjournals.org/content/36/3/837)

### Evidence against the claim

- Snopes rated the popular version of this claim ("spicy peppers cure breast cancer") as unproven, noting capsaicin "does have cancer fighting properties in the lab, but its use as an anti-cancer therapy in humans is far from certain." (https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/spicy-peppers-breast-cancer/)
- A 2023 review in *Frontiers in Oncology* states the "clinical value of per os capsaicin to complement chemotherapy is still speculative." (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10177684/)
- Notably, capsaicin may have **pro-tumor effects**: Erin et al. found capsaicin-induced sensory neuron inactivation *promoted* a more aggressive phenotype and enhanced metastasis in a murine breast cancer model. (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10549-006-9219-7)

### Bottom line

Capsaicin is a plausible candidate for adjunct cancer research, but no human clinical trial has demonstrated that it treats breast cancer. Anyone considering it should consult an oncologist; it is not a validated treatment.
